back: Formation of microspores from a pollen mother cell through meiosis. It occurs in the microsporangium of the anther and ends in a microspore tetrad.
Each microspore of the tetrad is haploid (n), because it is a product of meiosis of the diploid pollen mother cell.

front: Four wall layers of the microsporangium
back: Epidermis, endothecium, middle layers and tapetum. The outer three protect the sporangium and help in dehiscence; the tapetum nourishes the pollen grains.
Innermost wall layer of the microsporangium. Its cells have dense cytoplasm and usually more than one nucleus, and they nourish the developing pollen grains.
Hard outer wall made of sporopollenin, one of the most resistant organic materials known. It resists high temperature, strong acids and alkali, and bears germ pores where sporopollenin is absent.
Thin, continuous inner wall of the pollen grain, made of cellulose and pectin.

front: Two cells of a mature pollen grain
back: A large vegetative cell with abundant food reserve and an irregular nucleus, and a small spindle-shaped generative cell that floats in its cytoplasm.
Highly variable and dependent on temperature and humidity. Rice and wheat pollen loses viability within 30 minutes; some Rosaceae, Leguminoseae and Solanaceae keep it for months.
Pollen of many species stored for years in liquid nitrogen at minus 196 degrees Celsius, used in crop breeding programmes like a seed bank.
Formation of the female gametophyte from a single functional megaspore, the other three megaspores having degenerated. Usual in a majority of flowering plants.
Formation of megaspores from the megaspore mother cell in the nucellus of the ovule, by meiosis. It yields four megaspores, of which one is functional.

front: Structure of the mature embryo sac
back: 7-celled and 8-nucleate: egg apparatus of two synergids and one egg cell at the micropylar end, three antipodals at the chalazal end, and a large central cell with two polar nuclei.
Special cellular thickenings at the micropylar tip of the synergids. It guides the pollen tube into the synergid.
Pollination within the same flower, from anther to stigma of the same flower. Complete autogamy is rare in flowers that open and expose their anthers and stigma.
Transfer of pollen from anther to stigma of another flower of the same plant. Functionally cross-pollination, but genetically similar to autogamy.
Transfer of pollen from anther to stigma of a different plant. It is the only pollination type that brings genetically different pollen grains to the stigma.
Flowers that never open. Anthers dehisce inside the bud and pollinate the stigma of the same flower, so they are invariably autogamous and set seed without pollinators.
A genetic mechanism that prevents self-pollen from fertilising the ovules by inhibiting pollen germination on the stigma or pollen tube growth in the style.
All events from pollen deposition on the stigma until the pollen tube enters the ovule. The pistil recognises compatible pollen and accepts it, or rejects incompatible pollen.
Removal of anthers from a flower bud before the anther dehisces, using forceps, when the female parent has bisexual flowers. It prevents self-pollination in artificial hybridisation.
Covering an emasculated flower with a butter paper bag so that unwanted pollen cannot reach the stigma. Done before the stigma becomes receptive and repeated after pollination.
Two fusions in the same embryo sac: syngamy of one male gamete with the egg, and triple fusion of the other male gamete with the two polar nuclei. Unique to flowering plants.
Syngamy gives the diploid zygote. Triple fusion gives the triploid primary endosperm nucleus, which forms the primary endosperm cell and then the endosperm.
The primary endosperm nucleus divides repeatedly to give free nuclei, and cell walls are laid down later. Coconut water is free-nuclear endosperm; the white kernel is cellular endosperm.
Albuminous seeds retain part of the endosperm in the mature seed, as in wheat, maize, barley and castor. Non-albuminous seeds have none left, as in pea and groundnut.
The residual, persistent nucellus left in some seeds, such as black pepper and beet.
The single cotyledon of a grass embryo, situated laterally on the embryonal axis.
In a grass embryo, the coleoptile is the hollow foliar sheath around the shoot apex and leaf primordia; the coleorrhiza is the sheath around the radicle and root cap.
A fruit in which the thalamus also contributes to fruit formation along with the ovary, as in apple, strawberry and cashew. A fruit from the ovary alone is a true fruit.
Development of fruit without fertilisation, giving seedless fruit, as in banana. It can be induced by applying growth hormones.
A mechanism, found in some Asteraceae and grasses, that produces seeds without fertilisation. It is asexual reproduction that mimics sexual reproduction.
Occurrence of more than one embryo in a seed, as when nucellar cells around the embryo sac divide and grow into embryos in Citrus and mango.
